match.reason: Neither bank point teaches the same idea: the new point is a focused reader-rereading step (finding unclear parts, missing evidence and cuts before polishing), while the bank points cover broader revise-versus-polish drafting or a set of sentence-level revision techniques, so a new point fits better.

draft.title: Revising for a reader
card: Revising means rereading your draft as your audience would. Read it as someone who has not seen your plan and knows only what is on the page.
mark any sentence where a reader might have to stop and guess what you mean. Fix these first.
mark any claim a reader could doubt. Add an example, a fact or a quotation to support it.
mark any part that repeats a point or does not help your purpose. Taking it out makes the piece stronger.
draft.remember: Revise for the reader first: clear, supported and focused. Polish the wording last.

a.q: Which action is revising for a reader?
opts: Marking a doubtful claim and adding an example
Replacing plain words with longer words to sound formal
Checking each comma and apostrophe is in the right place
Changing the font and spacing so the page looks neat
a.why: Revising means rereading as the audience and finding where they would doubt a claim, so an example is added. Swapping words and fixing punctuation are polishing the language, which comes later.
a.clue: Which action starts from what the reader needs?

b.q: Ayla rereads her speech about a school canteen. She sees that two paragraphs make the same point and that one claim has no support. What should she do before polishing her word choices?
opts: Cut one repeated paragraph and add support for the claim
Add more adjectives to the repeated paragraphs
Fix the spelling and then read it aloud once
Keep both paragraphs so the speech is longer
b.why: Cutting repeated material and supporting the doubtful claim are revision for a reader, and they come first. Adding adjectives and fixing spelling are polishing, so they come after the bigger problems are fixed.
b.clue: Fix what the reader would question or skip before touching the wording.

a.best: Marking a doubtful claim and adding an example

b.best: Cut one repeated paragraph and add support for the claim
